title: GitHub Actions: Automating Workflows
description: Build and trigger automated workflows using GitHub Actions with reusable components and secrets.

data.text: **GitHub Actions** is a CI/CD platform built into GitHub that lets you automate your build, test, and deployment workflows. Workflows are defined as YAML files stored in your repository, making them versioned and reviewable alongside your code.

terms.definition: A configurable set of automated tasks you can run in response to events in your repository.
A set of steps that execute on the same runner.
An individual task within a job that can run commands, use an action, or run a script.
A reusable, shareable package that performs a specific task (e.g., setup Node.js, send a Slack message).
A server that runs workflows when triggered. GitHub-hosted or self-hosted.

cards.title: Workflow
cards.description: A collection of jobs triggered by an event. Defined in a YAML file.

cards.title: Job
cards.description: A set of steps that execute on the same runner.

cards.title: Step
cards.description: An individual task within a job — either a command or an action.

data.text: Workflows are triggered by events. The most common triggers are defined under the `on:` key at the top of the workflow file.

data.title: Common triggers
data.content: Trigger workflows on push, pull request, manual dispatch, or on a schedule.
data.code:
# Push and PR to main branch
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

# Manual trigger
on:
  workflow_dispatch:

# Scheduled (cron)
:on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 6 * * *' # Every day at 6 AM UTC

# On issue or release
on:
  issues:
    types: [opened, closed]
  release:
    types: [published]

data.title: Build, test, and deploy a Node.js app
data.content: This workflow builds and tests a Node.js app on every push, then deploys on release.
data.code:
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '20'
        cache: 'npm'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Lint
      run: npm run lint

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test

    - name: Build
      run: npm run build

    - name: Upload build artifacts
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: dist
        path: dist/

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Deploy to staging
      run: |
        echo 'Deploying to staging...'
        # Add your deploy commands here

data.text: GitHub Actions supports any language with a runner. For .NET applications, use `actions/setup-dotnet` and `dotnet` CLI commands.

data.title: .NET build workflow
data.content: A complete CI/CD pipeline for a C# .NET 8 web application.
data.code:
name: .NET CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Setup .NET
      uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
      with:
        dotnet-version: '8.0.x'

    - name: Restore dependencies
      run: dotnet restore

    - name: Build
      run: dotnet build --no-restore

    - name: Run tests
      run: dotnet test --no-build --verbosity normal

    - name: Publish
      run: dotnet publish -c Release -o out/

    - name: Upload artifacts
      uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
      with:
        name: app
        path: out/

data.text: Each step either runs a shell command (`run:`) or uses a pre-built action (`uses:`). Actions from the GitHub Marketplace (like `actions/checkout` or `actions/setup-node`) save you from writing boilerplate. The `needs:` keyword creates job dependencies, and `if:` adds conditional execution.

data.text: As your workflows grow, you can factor out common logic into **reusable workflows** and **composite actions**. This keeps your pipelines DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself).

data.title: Reusable workflow
data.content: Define a reusable workflow that other workflows can call with `uses:`.
data.code:
name: Reusable Build

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      node-version:
        required: false
        type: string
        default: '20'

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

data.title: Calling a reusable workflow
data.content: Reuse the build workflow from another workflow file.

data.title: Use workflow_run for downstream pipelines
data.text: You can chain workflows using `workflow_run` to trigger a deployment workflow after a CI workflow completes. This keeps your build and deploy pipelines separate.
GitHub stores secrets encrypted and provides them to workflows as environment variables. Add them under your repo's **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions**.

data.title: Using secrets in a workflow
data.content: Reference secrets with the ${{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }} syntax.

data.title: Never log secrets
data.text: GitHub automatically masks secrets in logs, but you should still avoid printing them. Never write `echo $SECRET` or pass secrets directly in commands.
For production deployments, use **environments** with required reviewers and deployment branches. This adds a manual approval gate before deploying to production.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: GitHub Actions automates CI/CD workflows using YAML files in your repo.
Workflows consist of jobs, which consist of steps — each step runs a command or uses an action.
Reuse common patterns with reusable workflows and composite actions.
Store secrets in GitHub and reference them with `${{ secrets.NAME }}`; never print them.
Use environments and required reviewers for production deployment gates.
data.takeaway: GitHub Actions brings CI/CD to your GitHub workflow — version-controlled pipelines with powerful automation.
